ocar.opportunity: Synapse-level electron-microscopy connectomes map wiring, but they usually omit the molecular identities of neurons, including neuromodulators that reshape circuit output.
ocar.challenge: Existing genetic tags, CLEM, and immunoEM approaches are hard to multiplex across a large serial-section series, so chemical identity and synaptic maps stay poorly overlaid.
ocar.action: Shahidi, Williams, Jékely and colleagues introduce serial multiplex immunogold labeling (siGOLD): immunogold-label small subsets of sections within a larger ssTEM series, then reconstruct the tagged neurons.
ocar.resolution: They apply 11 neuropeptide antibodies to a full-body larval Platynereis ssTEM dataset (HT9-4), reconstruct peptidergic neurons, and recover nuchal-organ circuitry expressing pigment-dispersing factor.
ocar.future_work: The method is presented as a way to overlay chemical neuromodulatory maps onto synaptic connectomes; it depends on continuous high-quality series and markers that label along neurites.

summaries.beginner: Connectome maps show which neurons touch, but they usually do not say what chemical messengers those cells use. This paper tags neuropeptides with gold particles on just a few electron-microscope slices so the same cells can be followed through a whole larval worm.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015), Shahidi and colleagues combine serial multiplex immunogold labeling (siGOLD) with serial-section TEM to assign molecular identities to peptidergic neurons. Because neuropeptides are highly immunogenic and travel along axons, they immunolabel small subsets of sections within a larger series and still recover whole-cell morphologies. They demonstrate scalability with 11 neuropeptide antibodies on a full-body Platynereis larva and reconstruct nuchal-organ circuitry that siGOLD finds expressing pigment-dispersing factor, a circadian neuropeptide.
summaries.advanced: siGOLD is shown for neuropeptides, not for arbitrary cytoplasmic antigens: the authors argue it needs markers that label along neurites so sparse sections still hit the cell. The selected text does not report quantitative labeling efficiency, false-positive rates, or how many neurons were recovered per antibody. Reconstruction still requires a continuous ssTEM series of sufficient quality to trace neurites across unlabeled gaps. Catalog metadata lists the venue as bioRxiv; the PDF is the eLife version of record.

plain_language_summary: Connectome maps show which neurons touch, but they usually do not say what chemical messengers those cells use. This paper tags neuropeptides with gold particles on just a few electron-microscope slices so the same cells can be followed through a whole larval worm.

ocar.opportunity: Automated reconstruction of neural circuits from electron-microscopy images needs community benchmarks that can turn competing segmentation algorithms into a shared progress metric.
ocar.challenge: Before this challenge, 2D EM boundary detection lacked a public, expert-consensus test set, so it was hard to know which algorithms actually helped connectomics.
ocar.action: Arganda-Carreras, Turaga, Seung and colleagues organized the first international 2D EM segmentation challenge: teams submitted boundary maps for a held-out test set scored against a consensus of human expert annotations.
ocar.resolution: The winning team had no prior EM experience and used a convolutional network; deep learning then became a standard for EM segmentation, and later the best result came from cooperation between two teams.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue the 2D challenge has probably saturated because of scoring ambiguities and test-set size, and they propose a scoring fix for neurite-border width variation aimed at a future 3D challenge.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to outline every nerve fiber in electron-microscope pictures of brain. This group ran the first public contest for that 2D outlining task, and a deep-learning team with no prior electron-microscopy experience won.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2015), Arganda-Carreras and colleagues report the ISBI 2D EM segmentation challenge. Participants submitted predicted boundary maps scored against a consensus of expert annotations; the winning IDSIA convolutional-network entry had no prior EM experience and helped establish deep learning as a standard. The challenge continued to accept submissions, with the best result at the time coming from two cooperating teams. Retrospective analysis found the scoring system was not robust to variations in neurite-border width.
summaries.advanced: The authors state that current best error rates of 1–2% remain far too high for fully automated scientific reconstructions, which they argue need nuisance error rates averaging less than one mistake per neuron. They also say 2D scoring and a small test set cap further progress. The selected extract does not name the winning F-score or list per-team numerical ranks. Training labels were by Cardona; the test set was labeled by Berger and Arganda-Carreras.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to outline every nerve fiber in electron-microscope pictures of brain. This group ran the first public contest for that 2D outlining task, and a deep-learning team with no prior electron-microscopy experience won.

ocar.opportunity: Developmental programs can build circuits with matching structure and function across individuals, but how similar an entire sensory-motor connectome is from animal to animal is rarely measured at synapse resolution.
ocar.challenge: Prior work had reconstructed the Platynereis larval visual circuit in one specimen (HT9-3), leaving open whether cell types, projections, and even left–right synaptic asymmetries would recur in a second larva.
ocar.action: Randel, Shahidi, Jékely and colleagues acquire a full-body ssTEM volume of a second 72 hpf Platynereis larva (HT9-4) and reconstruct the visual-eye and eyespot connectomes for quantitative comparison.
ocar.resolution: Cell complement, neuronal projections, and synaptic connectivity are highly stereotyped between individuals, including left–right connectivity asymmetries in some neurons, supporting a hard-wired larval eye circuit.
ocar.future_work: The authors conclude that reconstructions from more than one individual can greatly benefit connectome projects.

summaries.beginner: Scientists had mapped the visual wiring of one marine-worm larva and wondered whether the next animal would match. A second whole-body electron-microscope volume shows the same cell types, paths, and even some left–right wiring quirks.
summaries.intermediate: In an eLife Research Advance (2015), Randel and colleagues report a full-body ssTEM dataset of a 72 hpf Platynereis larva (HT9-4): 5,056 sections at 40 nm thickness and 5.7 nm/pixel, with some neuropil re-imaged at 2.22 nm/pixel. They reconstruct circuitry downstream of the four visual eyes and the larval eyespots and compare it with the earlier HT9-3 head volume. Anatomical and quantitative analyses show high inter-individual stereotypy of cell complement, projections, and synapses, including left–right connectivity asymmetries.
summaries.advanced: They lost 1.9% of sections (98 layers), with the three biggest gaps spanning five sections, plus 113 unimaged layers; tracing used local and global cues. 164 fragments could not be traced (100 < 4 μm, 46 of 4–40 μm, 18 > 40 μm). Stereotypy analysis is mainly on neuronal groups using average synapse numbers, and weakly connected sensory neurons plus cells presynaptic to the eye circuit were excluded. The claim is hard-wiring of this larval eye circuit, not whole-nervous-system stereotypy.

plain_language_summary: Scientists had mapped the visual wiring of one marine-worm larva and wondered whether the next animal would match. A second whole-body electron-microscope volume shows the same cell types, paths, and even some left–right wiring quirks.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes start from over-segmented superpixels that must be clustered into neurons; better agglomeration would cut the manual correction that still dominates reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Standard agglomerative methods mix biologically different superpixels (for example mitochondria versus neurites) and make greedy merge decisions that can lock in boundary errors.
ocar.action: Parag, Chakraborty, Plaza, and Scheffer propose context-aware delayed agglomeration (CADA): split superpixels of different biological entities into subsets, agglomerate them separately, and postpone some merge decisions on newly formed bodies.
ocar.resolution: They report significant accuracy gains over standard methods on 2D and 3D datasets; a CADA-L variant needs substantially fewer training examples, and application to fly-medulla FIB-SEM volumes yielded an estimated ~30% reduction in subsequent manual correction time.
ocar.future_work: They point to interactive training of pixel and superpixel-boundary classifiers as a route to drop exhaustive ground truth when scaling reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Automatic neuron tracing often glues the wrong bits together, especially when mitochondria and nerve fibers look similar. This method sorts those bits into biological categories first and waits on shaky merge decisions, which the authors say cuts later human cleanup.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2015 arXiv version of work catalogued as PLoS ONE (2014), Parag and colleagues introduce a context-aware delayed agglomeration framework for EM segmentation. After watershed-style oversegmentation, superpixels of different biological entities are agglomerated separately, and a delayed clustering scheme postpones some merges to improve boundary prediction. They compare against GALA and other baselines, highlighting reduced over- and under-segmentation, and apply the method to 216 FIB-SEM volumes at 10 nm isotropic resolution from the fly medulla.
summaries.advanced: The ~30% reduction in subsequent manual correction time is an estimate versus Takemura et al. on two of the 5,203-voxel-scale blocks, not a blinded multi-annotator trial reported here. CADA-L’s training-set efficiency is argued qualitatively (fewer examples, no extra iterations) rather than as a single headline metric in the selected extract. Interactive training with as few as <20% of examples is cited from a companion paper, not fully evaluated here. The extract does not report a single variation-of-information number for the 216-volume run.

plain_language_summary: Automatic neuron tracing often glues the wrong bits together, especially when mitochondria and nerve fibers look similar. This method sorts those bits into biological categories first and waits on shaky merge decisions, which the authors say cuts later human cleanup.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput serial-section EM now yields nanoscale volumes in which neurons and synapses are in principle visible, so an end-to-end path from images to a brain graph is newly conceivable.
ocar.challenge: Prior algorithms optimized isolated tasks such as neuron segmentation or synapse detection, not the quality of the resulting connectivity graph, and none produced a graph without human interaction.
ocar.action: Gray Roncal, Kleissas, Vogelstein, Hager and colleagues present a fully automated images-to-graphs pipeline, introduce a graph-error metric to choose algorithms and parameters, and deploy a reference version on a large public dataset.
ocar.resolution: They recast reconstruction as graph estimation, search operating points for the best available brain graph under their metric, and release code and data derivatives as a community baseline.
ocar.future_work: They note the metric currently treats binary unweighted graphs, and they flag extensions to attributed graphs, error-type weighting, and analysis of bias in errors as next steps.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stacks of brain can in principle become wiring diagrams, but most software only solves one step, such as coloring cells or finding synapses. This paper strings those steps into a fully automatic pipeline that outputs a graph and scores how good that graph is.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2015), Gray Roncal and colleagues describe what they present as the first fully automated images-to-graphs pipeline for high-resolution EM connectomics—no human interaction from imaged volume to brain graph. They introduce a graph error metric to select algorithms and parameters, evaluate combinations of published and novel modules, and deploy a reference end-to-end version on a large public dataset. Code and data derivatives are released through the Open Connectome Project infrastructure.
summaries.advanced: The authors stress that automated graphs need not be perfect to support statistical inference, but they do not claim biologically complete reconstructions. The selected extract does not report numerical graph-error scores, volume size, or which public dataset was the reference run. The metric is binary and unweighted; bias in error types is explicitly not fully explored. EM data and truth labels are acknowledged from Kasthuri, Berger, and Lichtman.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stacks of brain can in principle become wiring diagrams, but most software only solves one step, such as coloring cells or finding synapses. This paper strings those steps into a fully automatic pipeline that outputs a graph and scores how good that graph is.

ocar.opportunity: Chemical synapses are the edges of an EM connectome, and larger volumes make exhaustive manual synapse annotation a rate-limiting step once neurite tracing is automated.
ocar.challenge: A Drosophila brain contains tens of millions of synapses that would take years to mark by hand; contactomes based on membrane apposition can mislead relative to stained, annotated synapses.
ocar.action: Plaza, Parag, Huang, Rivlin and colleagues build a semi-automated workflow: automatically predict T-bars, then have proofreaders validate predictions and trace postsynaptic partners in seven Drosophila medulla columns.
ocar.resolution: A 4–6 person team finished the volume in six months; T-bar density is higher in proximal layers (maximum densities over twice the minima) while PSDs per T-bar stay more consistent with depth.
ocar.future_work: They argue the workflow is crowd-sourceable, that better T-bar and PSD algorithms plus visualization could speed it further, and that neuropil with many synapses per partner pair might eventually allow higher-precision, lower-recall automation.

summaries.beginner: Finding every synapse in a large electron-microscope volume can take years if people scan every slice. This team has a computer guess the presynaptic T-bars in fly medulla and then asks humans to check them and mark partners, finishing a seven-column volume in months rather than years.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2014 arXiv preprint, Plaza and colleagues annotate synapses throughout seven Drosophila medulla columns in a 40 × 40 × 50 µm-scale volume sampled at 10 nm per voxel. An automatic detector proposes T-bars; a Raveler workflow then validates those sites and traces postsynaptic densities. With a 4–6 person proofreader team they completed the volume in six months. They also treat synapse maps as a constraint for later segmentation and as a way to see compartment structure across columns.
summaries.advanced: The authors state that T-bar annotation is not the time bottleneck; PSD tracing remains slow despite protocol improvements. The selected extract gives a table average of 73.6 without a clear unit in the truncated caption, so that figure is not interpreted here. They note that even perfect prediction would still require verification if every site is examined. Dataset size is written as “40x40x50 m” in the extract; context (seven medulla columns, 10 nm voxels) indicates a micrometre-scale slab, not metres.

plain_language_summary: Finding every synapse in a large electron-microscope volume can take years if people scan every slice. This team has a computer guess the presynaptic T-bars in fly medulla and then asks humans to check them and mark partners, finishing a seven-column volume in months rather than years.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentations of connectomic volumes still need hundreds of human corrections per cubic micron, so proofreading tools that make split, merge, and boundary edits fast and usable are essential.
ocar.challenge: Existing proofreading software had not been compared head-to-head for accuracy, speed, and usability when non-experts correct neurons in public connectomics data.
ocar.action: Haehn, Knowles-Barley, Pfister and colleagues present Mojo, a single-user desktop proofreading application, and Dojo, a multi-user web tool, and run a between-subjects user study against Janelia’s Raveler.
ocar.resolution: Given the same time, non-experts using web-based Dojo made significantly more corrections and all Dojo users reported better usability; the paper analyzes requirements for visual proofreading software.
ocar.future_work: The study is framed as design guidance for future proofreading interfaces rather than as a claim that any tool removes the need for expert review.

summaries.beginner: Computers outline cells in electron-microscope stacks, but people still have to fix many mistakes. This paper builds two correction tools—one on the desktop, one in a web browser—and finds that non-experts fix more errors with the web tool in the same amount of time.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2014), Haehn and colleagues describe Mojo (fully featured single-user desktop proofreading) and Dojo (collaborative web-based proofreading) for connectomic EM segmentations. They run a between-subjects experiment in which non-experts proofread neurons in a public dataset, comparing accuracy and speed with Raveler. Web-based Dojo yielded a significant improvement in corrections given equal time, and all Dojo participants reported better usability.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract does not report participant count, volume size, or the numeric size of the Dojo advantage. Claims of “hundreds of corrections per cubic micron” come from the abstract’s problem statement, not from a new measurement in this extract. The bundled PDF extract is a different paper (Lauenburg et al., SynAnno, 2025 bioRxiv) and was not used; this card is grounded in the catalog abstract for Haehn et al. 2014.

plain_language_summary: Computers outline cells in electron-microscope stacks, but people still have to fix many mistakes. This paper builds two correction tools—one on the desktop, one in a web browser—and finds that non-experts fix more errors with the web tool in the same amount of time.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution connectomics needs both more accurate automatic EM segmentation and a way to send proofreaders to the voxels most likely to be wrong, rather than forcing them to inspect every voxel.
ocar.challenge: Even state-of-the-art agglomeration was still far too inaccurate to reconstruct a neuron without errors, and humans still had to examine the entire volume.
ocar.action: Nunez-Iglesias, Kennedy, Plaza, Chakraborty, and Katz present gala, a Python library implementing graph-based active learning of agglomeration, built on the scientific Python stack.
ocar.resolution: They report state-of-the-art agglomerative segmentation plus pointers to likely error coordinates, with anecdotal 5–16-fold speedups in proofreading, and they document library architecture and current limitations.
ocar.future_work: They intend to address software limitations and to explore gala on 3D light microscopy and 3D+t neuronal activity data.

summaries.beginner: Automatic coloring of neurons in electron-microscope volumes still makes many mistakes, and people usually have to look at every pixel to find them. This Python library both improves the automatic coloring and highlights the spots most likely to be wrong.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2014), Nunez-Iglesias and colleagues describe gala (graph-based active learning of agglomeration), a Python library using numpy, scipy, networkx, scikit-learn, and scikit-image. Building on their 2013 algorithm, gala repeatedly consults a gold-standard segmentation to learn agglomeration and to flag likely errors. They present the software architecture, designs they consider reusable, and limitations they plan to address. Anecdotal FlyEM use suggested 5–16-fold faster proofreading.
summaries.advanced: The 5–16-fold speedup is explicitly anecdotal, not a controlled timing study in this methods paper. The selected extract does not report numerical segmentation scores versus named baselines. GALA still depends on a gold-standard segmentation for training. Catalog and PDF agree on the 2014 Frontiers article; the underlying agglomeration algorithm is cited as Nunez-Iglesias et al. 2013.

plain_language_summary: Automatic coloring of neurons in electron-microscope volumes still makes many mistakes, and people usually have to look at every pixel to find them. This Python library both improves the automatic coloring and highlights the spots most likely to be wrong.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM acquisition now makes synaptic-resolution maps of even large mammalian brains conceivable, turning connectomics into a data-driven field analogous to early genomics.
ocar.challenge: The field produces unprecedented volumes of digital data at unprecedented rates; turning raw images into minable wiring maps—not the imaging itself—is the hard part.
ocar.action: Lichtman, Pfister, and Shavit survey key computational and infrastructural difficulties after data acquisition and offer suggestions for managing them.
ocar.resolution: They frame both petabyte-scale image data and terabyte-scale reconstructed graphs as digital brains whose scientific value depends on how easily they can be mined, and they argue success requires biologists, engineers, and computer scientists on equal footing.
ocar.future_work: They note that even cortical graphs of a small mammal can reach several terabytes, creating another uncharted big-data problem, and that commercial or health applications may be needed to fund the investment.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring maps are starting to produce enormous computer files, more like genome projects than like classic microscope papers. This commentary argues that storing and turning those pictures into searchable maps is now harder than taking the pictures.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2014), Lichtman, Pfister, and Shavit review the big-data challenges of synaptic-resolution connectomics. They note that mapping began with a worm in the 1970s and that automated EM now raises the prospect of large mammalian brains, generating perhaps petabyte-scale structural datasets. Drawing on their own experience, they argue the post-acquisition pipeline—alignment, reconstruction, storage, and mining—needs breakthrough algorithms, analogous to genomics. Conclusions emphasize cost, interdisciplinary teams, and neuromorphic or clinical motivations.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a methods benchmark: no new reconstruction accuracy numbers are presented. Scale claims (petabytes of images, terabytes of graphs) are order-of-magnitude framing. The authors explicitly say it is unclear whether the field succeeds without a clear commercial or health application. The “beyond the horizon” problem is analyzing the graphs themselves once they exist.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring maps are starting to produce enormous computer files, more like genome projects than like classic microscope papers. This commentary argues that storing and turning those pictures into searchable maps is now harder than taking the pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Small but biologically interesting circuits have been reconstructed and used to extract functional insight, showing that connectomes can be more than anatomy catalogs.
ocar.challenge: Those reconstructions were heroic proofs of concept, requiring person-months of effort per neuron, and will not scale to larger circuits or whole-animal brains.
ocar.action: Plaza, Scheffer, and Chklovskii examine what larger connectomes will require and highlight five areas needing attention.
ocar.resolution: They call for imaging better suited to automatic reconstruction with excellent z-resolution; automatic synapse detection, validation, and measurement; uncertainty metrics kept for every object through the pipeline; fully incremental processes so partial connectomes are usable; and better analysis tools once graphs exist.
ocar.future_work: The review is a roadmap for scaling reconstruction rather than a report of a new dataset.

summaries.beginner: A few tiny circuits have been wired out by hand, but that pace cannot reach a whole brain. This review lists the imaging, synapse-finding, uncertainty-tracking, and analysis changes needed before large connectomes become routine.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2014), Plaza, Scheffer, and Chklovskii argue that existing connectome reconstructions will not scale. They identify five priorities: imaging with excellent z-resolution suited to automatic reconstruction; automatic synapse detection, validation, and measurement; methods that carry uncertainty from images through segmentation and queries; incremental pipelines that yield usable partial connectomes; and better tools to analyze connectomes once obtained.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/roadmap article; the abstract does not quantify person-months per neuron beyond that qualitative claim, nor name the circuits used as examples. The bundled PDF extract is a different paper (Makarova et al., eLife 2025, on a Megaphragma compound-eye FIB-SEM reconstruction) and was not used; this card is grounded in the catalog abstract for Plaza et al. 2014.

plain_language_summary: A few tiny circuits have been wired out by hand, but that pace cannot reach a whole brain. This review lists the imaging, synapse-finding, uncertainty-tracking, and analysis changes needed before large connectomes become routine.

ocar.opportunity: Teravoxel EM connectomics volumes and their segmentations are too large for conventional visualization, yet neuroscientists need to ask domain-specific questions on the full data.
ocar.challenge: General-purpose query languages and small-crop viewers do not let collaborators pose stepwise, knowledge-based queries while seeing EM, segmentation, connectivity, and metadata together.
ocar.action: Beyer, Al-Awami, Kasthuri, Lichtman, Pfister, and Hadwiger present ConnectomeExplorer: a visual query algebra plus a scalable volume-visualization framework, with a visual query builder that composes complex queries from simpler ones.
ocar.resolution: On roughly one terabyte of EM data and 750 GB of segmentation—over 4,000 segmented structures and 1,000 synapses—collaborators answered scientific questions on the full-size data for the first time.
ocar.future_work: They want to integrate more advanced segmentation and proofreading, research 3D navigation for petascale volumes, and extend the system toward comparative visualization of query results.

summaries.beginner: A terabyte of brain electron-microscope data is too big to explore by scrolling around. This software lets neuroscientists build questions step by step and see the answers on the real volume, the colored cells, and the wiring at once.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2013), Beyer and colleagues introduce ConnectomeExplorer, combining a knowledge-based query algebra with visualization that scales to multiple volumes of several teravoxels. Queries are specified interactively in a visual builder. They evaluate on ~1 TB of EM data and 750 GB of segmentation containing over 4,000 segmented structures and 1,000 synapses, enabling collaborators to query and analyze the full-size data.
summaries.advanced: The knowledge-based algebra is intentionally less general than SQL or MATLAB; the authors treat that as a usability advantage but note that complex dynamic queries still need training. Early attempts to show connectivity as a 2D graph inside the 3D volume were dropped after collaborator feedback in favor of a separate graph view. The paper reports that collaborators discovered previously unknown facts about their dataset but the selected extract does not list those biological findings in quantitative detail.

plain_language_summary: A terabyte of brain electron-microscope data is too big to explore by scrolling around. This software lets neuroscientists build questions step by step and see the answers on the real volume, the colored cells, and the wiring at once.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM can acquire gigabyte-to-terabyte image volumes, so 3D reconstructions of neuronal processes at nanometre scale are limited mainly by segmentation, not by imaging.
ocar.challenge: Pipelines that work on small crops often fail to stay geometrically consistent or computationally tractable across hundreds of sections of mammalian neuropil.
ocar.action: Kaynig, Vazquez-Reina, Pfister and colleagues train a random-forest classifier on interactive sparse annotations, combine it with an anisotropic smoothing prior in a CRF to propose multiple 2D hypotheses, then fuse those hypotheses into 3D objects; they also introduce Mojo for scribble-based merge correction.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate reconstructions from a 27,000 μm³ mammalian volume (30 μm on a side; 1,000 sections; 25 GB at 8 bits) and provide qualitative and quantitative automatic-segmentation evaluation.
ocar.future_work: They planned to drop MATLAB dependencies, improve runtime and segmentation, and build a web-based Mojo for collaborative proofreading.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope stacks of brain are now easy to take but hard to turn into 3D cell shapes. This pipeline learns from a few human scribbles, proposes outlines on each slice, glues them into 3D objects, and offers a tool to fix leftover merges.
summaries.intermediate: In work later published in Medical Image Analysis (catalog 2013/2015; arXiv 2013 extract), Kaynig and colleagues present a GB–TB-scale reconstruction pipeline: a random forest trained on interactive sparse labels, a CRF with an anisotropic smoothing prior that yields multiple per-image hypotheses, and segmentation fusion into 3D processes. They reconstruct neuronal processes from a 27,000 μm³ cube (30 μm × 30 μm × 1,000 sections; 5,120 × 5,120 pixels; 25 GB). Mojo supports semi-automated merge correction from sparse user scribbles.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract claims state-of-the-art reconstruction performance but does not quote a variation-of-information or split/merge table in the truncated text. Volume geometry is 30 μm in each dimension with 1,000 sections; pixel size is given as 5,210 or 5,120 pixels depending on figure versus caption, so linear resolution in nm/pixel is not restated here. Mojo in this paper addresses merge errors via scribbles, not a full collaborative web client (that is listed as future work).

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope stacks of brain are now easy to take but hard to turn into 3D cell shapes. This pipeline learns from a few human scribbles, proposes outlines on each slice, glues them into 3D objects, and offers a tool to fix leftover merges.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience is expanding rapidly, yet many brain diseases still lack tissue-level signs, suggesting that the physically distinctive structure of neural circuits is under-measured.
ocar.challenge: Critics argue that synaptic wiring maps are too expensive, too slow, or theoretically uninformative; Morgan and Lichtman take those objections seriously but reject the conclusion that connectomics should not be done.
ocar.action: They argue that albeit limitations, synapse-resolution maps will reveal essential circuit characteristics inaccessible to sparse cellular sampling.
ocar.resolution: They give three reasons: experience-dependent connectivity patterns cannot be seen a few cells at a time; systems physiology remains a black box without the network level; and dense structural exploration is likely to reveal unexpected properties.
ocar.future_work: The essay is a justification for undertaking connectomics despite cost and incompleteness, not a methods paper with a reconstruction target.

summaries.beginner: Some scientists think mapping every synapse is a bad investment. This essay says those maps will show wiring patterns that no handful of recordings can see, and that without them the gap between single cells and whole-brain function stays a black box.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Morgan and Lichtman respond to skepticism about connectomics. They contrast the brain with other organs: many more cell types (the retina alone has more than 50 versus about five in liver), directional long-range synaptic partnerships, and circuit motifs without analogs in other tissues. They conclude that connectomic maps, despite limitations, will reveal essential circuit characteristics otherwise inaccessible.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion piece; the abstract is two sentences and the argument is conceptual. Cell-type counts (retina >50, liver closer to five) are cited from prior literature, not new measurements. The authors do not claim that a complete human connectome is imminent. Limitations of connectomics are acknowledged but not quantified (cost, time, or error rates).

plain_language_summary: Some scientists think mapping every synapse is a bad investment. This essay says those maps will show wiring patterns that no handful of recordings can see, and that without them the gap between single cells and whole-brain function stays a black box.

ocar.opportunity: Image-acquisition and processing advances were making large-scale synaptic circuit reconstruction newly plausible, inviting an ‘omics’ framing analogous to genomics.
ocar.challenge: The community was divided on whether wiring diagrams are feasible or even useful, echoing objections once raised against the Human Genome Project.
ocar.action: Lichtman and Sanes revisit the genome-project controversy to ask what lessons it holds for proposals to map the connectome.
ocar.resolution: They argue that studying brain function without cellular interconnection data may one day seem as odd as genetics without sequence, while remaining cautious that a single brain ‘connectome’ in the genomic sense may never exist.
ocar.future_work: They flag scale, variability, and stability as possibly insurmountable, yet still expect extensive public circuit data to matter for neuroscience, neurology, and psychiatry.

summaries.beginner: When genome sequencing was proposed, many people said it was too hard and not useful—until it became central to biology. This 2008 essay asks whether mapping brain wiring deserves the same kind of big, shared effort, while admitting brains may be more variable than genomes.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2008), Lichtman and Sanes compare connectomics with genomics. They note similar objections to feasibility and value, sketch a Cajal-to-circuits history, and ask whether mapping neural connections could ultimately have the same kind of value as sequencing genes. They define connectomics (playfully, via a dictionary-style entry) as high-speed structural mapping of neural circuits with databases and applications.
summaries.advanced: This is a pre-EM-boom opinion piece, not a reconstruction. The authors explicitly say it is premature to predict that a brain connectome will exist in the sense a genome exists; scale, variability, and stability may be insurmountable. No quantitative roadmap (cost, years, voxels) is offered in the selected text. The piece should be read as historical advocacy, not as evidence that those objections were fully answered.

plain_language_summary: When genome sequencing was proposed, many people said it was too hard and not useful—until it became central to biology. This 2008 essay asks whether mapping brain wiring deserves the same kind of big, shared effort, while admitting brains may be more variable than genomes.

ocar.opportunity: Community structure is a candidate organizing principle of connectomes, but it has rarely been measured in a whole brain mapped at single-neuron and synapse resolution.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether fine-scale communities in the adult Drosophila brain are spatially compact and assortative, how they relate to function, and whether reusable circuit archetypes exist.
ocar.action: Betzel, Puxeddu, Seguin and colleagues fit a nested stochastic blockmodel to a whole-brain adult fly connectome and then cluster communities into meta-clusters using spatial, functional, and molecular features.
ocar.resolution: Most of roughly 1,500 fine-scale communities are spatially compact, mostly assortative, and aligned with biological features; nonassortative communities concentrate in optic lobe and vision pathways; 45 archetypical meta-clusters are proposed as modular building blocks.
ocar.future_work: They discuss alternative feature sets for clustering, the conceptual limits of clustering clusters, and whether hierarchical and mixed assortative/non-assortative organization are shared across species and scales.

summaries.beginner: The fruit-fly whole-brain wiring map can be carved into neighborhoods of neurons that talk among themselves. This study finds about 1,500 small neighborhoods and then groups them into 45 repeating circuit styles, including some unusual mixing in the visual system.
summaries.intermediate: In a June 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Betzel and colleagues apply a nested stochastic blockmodel to an adult Drosophila whole-brain connectome. At the finest hierarchy level they report roughly 1,500 communities that are mostly spatially compact and assortative. Nonassortative communities co-localize in the optic lobe and vision-processing pathways. Data-driven clustering of community features yields 45 archetypical meta-clusters interpreted as functional primitives from which larger, more diverse communities are built.
summaries.advanced: This is an unreviewed preprint. The authors note that meta-clustering depends on the chosen feature set; principal components mitigate correlated features but not missing features. They argue neuron-level clustering would miss circuit-level properties, but that two-step clustering is conceptually delicate. Cross-species ‘universal principle’ language is framed as a candidate, not a demonstrated homology. The selected extract does not name which fly connectome release was used.

plain_language_summary: The fruit-fly whole-brain wiring map can be carved into neighborhoods of neurons that talk among themselves. This study finds about 1,500 small neighborhoods and then groups them into 45 repeating circuit styles, including some unusual mixing in the visual system.

ocar.opportunity: Mossy-fiber inputs onto CA3 pyramids are central to ideas about pattern separation, completion, and memory encoding, but there has been no large-scale synaptic wiring diagram of those connections.
ocar.challenge: Hippocampal axons and dendrites span millimetres, so small EM volumes cannot capture neuron identity together with mossy-fiber connectivity at synapse and vesicle resolution.
ocar.action: Zheng, Park, Hammerschmith, Seung, Tank and colleagues assemble a ~1 × 1 × 0.1 mm³ GridTape TEM volume of mouse CA3, proofread an automated segmentation, and classify all soma-containing neurons plus mossy-fiber axons.
ocar.resolution: They reconstruct 1,815 pyramidal cells, 229 inhibitory cells, and over 55,000 mossy-fiber axons; mossy-fiber input number follows a proximodistal gradient; shared inputs exceed degree-preserving nulls and better match proximity-preserving swaps; a feedforward inhibitory motif via perisomatic interneurons selectively targets a pyramidal subtype.
ocar.future_work: The dataset is shared on Pyr.ai; they contrast their 4-month-old female GridTape volume with a published CA3 EM volume that used a younger male, multi-beam SEM, and a more proximal subregion.

summaries.beginner: A famous hippocampal pathway was thought to help the brain tell similar memories apart, but nobody had a large wiring diagram of those contacts. This team reconstructs a millimetre-scale slab of mouse CA3 and finds a gradient of mossy-fiber inputs plus a selective inhibitory loop onto one pyramid type.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2026), Zheng and colleagues report a ~1 × 1 × 0.1 mm³ 3D EM volume of mouse hippocampal CA3 (2,048 serial TEM sections on GridTape). After proofreading they classify all soma-containing neurons—1,815 pyramidal and 229 inhibitory cells—and over 55,000 mossy-fiber axons. Thorny pyramids show a proximodistal gradient: proximal cells receive sparse large boutons, distal cells denser smaller terminals with fewer vesicles. Pyramids share more mossy-fiber axons than degree-preserving randomized networks. A feedforward inhibitory motif from mossy fibers via perisomatic interneurons selectively innervates a pyramidal subtype. Data are released on Pyr.ai.
summaries.advanced: Thorny versus sparsely thorny sublayers and distinct inhibitory axons are anatomical classifications; the paper discusses bursting and sharp-wave implications without claiming new in vivo physiology from this volume. Shared-input statistics depend on the chosen null models (degree-preserving versus proximity-preserving swaps). Comparison to Turner et al. notes differences in animal age/sex, imaging modality, targeted CA3 subregion, and sectioning plane. The selected extract does not quote a single p-value for the sharing test.

plain_language_summary: A famous hippocampal pathway was thought to help the brain tell similar memories apart, but nobody had a large wiring diagram of those contacts. This team reconstructs a millimetre-scale slab of mouse CA3 and finds a gradient of mossy-fiber inputs plus a selective inhibitory loop onto one pyramid type.

ocar.opportunity: Motif analysis can expose local building blocks of a fully reconstructed nervous system once connection signs (excitatory versus inhibitory) are available.
ocar.challenge: Unsigned motif counts ignore polarity; without a structure-preserving randomization that respects signs, overrepresented signed loops cannot be distinguished from wiring constraints.
ocar.action: Szilágyi, Gulyás, Csermely, Fenyves and colleagues perform what they present as the first edge-polarity-based signed motif analysis of the C. elegans connectome, using recent sign data and a novel structure-preserving randomization, including neuron-class coloring.
ocar.resolution: They identify 56 significantly overrepresented and 1 underrepresented three-node signed motifs; positive feedforward, negative feedback, disinhibitory feedback, and incoherent feedforward loops are overabundant, each with a characteristic sensory/motor layout.
ocar.future_work: They release a motif-enumeration tool and definition system intended for signed motif analysis in other complex networks.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s complete wiring diagram can now be read with plus and minus signs on the connections, not just lines. This study finds that certain three-cell loops—especially positive feedforward and negative feedback—show up more often than chance, with typical sensory-to-motor layouts.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2025 bioRxiv preprint (catalogued with a 2026 BMC Biology-style DOI), Szilágyi and colleagues run signed three-node motif analysis on the C. elegans neuronal network. Using connection-sign data and structure-preserving randomization, they report 56 overrepresented and one underrepresented signed motifs. Positive feedforward, negative feedback, disinhibitory feedback, and incoherent feedforward loops are highlighted as overabundant. Coloring nodes by modality (for example sensory versus motor) yields a characteristic neuronal layout for each significant loop.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists 2026 / BMC Biology-style DOI while the PDF is the January 2025 bioRxiv posting; treat version-of-record status as pending unless confirmed. Significance depends on the novel null model; the selected extract does not quote Z-score thresholds. The authors distinguish induced versus partial subgraphs in the introduction; which count underlies the 56+1 headline should be checked in the supplement (S4/S5). Functional roles of motifs (switches, and so on) are inferred from topology, not from new physiology.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s complete wiring diagram can now be read with plus and minus signs on the connections, not just lines. This study finds that certain three-cell loops—especially positive feedforward and negative feedback—show up more often than chance, with typical sensory-to-motor layouts.

ocar.opportunity: Axo-axonic synapses can veto, amplify, or synchronize spikes, but their circuit-scale organization in a complete ventral nerve cord was unknown.
ocar.challenge: Descending neurons carry brain commands into the cord; any chemical synapse onto those axons inside the cord is axo-axonic by definition, yet such contacts are rare and easy to miss in standard wiring summaries.
ocar.action: Ceballos, Pena and colleagues chart every axo-axonic input onto all 1,314 descending neurons in the adult male Drosophila MANC v1.2.1 connectome (23,665 cells), then test a predicted giant-fiber modulator cohort with immunostaining, modeling, and optogenetics.
ocar.resolution: High-degree neurons do not form an interconnected rich club; an octet of ascending neurons (AN08B098) makes exclusive giant-fiber (DNp01) contacts, is cholinergic, and increases DNp01 excitability when activated.
ocar.future_work: They note the map is one male, ignores gap junctions (undetected in this EM), uses leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics, and that some contacts could be dendro-axonic (about 2% of synapses in cited work).

summaries.beginner: Some synapses land on the outgoing cable of a neuron rather than on its branches, and can strongly change whether a spike leaves the brain. Using the fly’s ventral-cord wiring map, this team finds those contacts on descending neurons and shows that a small set of ascending cells can make the giant escape neurons easier to fire.
summaries.intermediate: In iScience (2026), Ceballos and colleagues use MANC v1.2.1 to list axo-axonic inputs onto 1,314 descending neurons. Highlights state such connections are rare in the VNC, that synapse number correlates with partner number, and that an AN08B098 octet connects exclusively with the giant fibers. Immunostaining supports a cholinergic identity; optogenetic activation increases DNp01 excitability, matching connectome-derived expectations. Network simulations complement the in vivo tests.
summaries.advanced: Limitations include a single male specimen (FANC/BANC not analyzed here), in silico whole-network tests plus optogenetics rather than large-scale physiology, LIF neurons that ignore conductance dynamics and neuromodulators, and absence of gap junctions in MANC EM. Gal4 lines labeled more cells than the AN08B098 connectome type; the authors cannot explain the mismatch. Mitochondria in presynaptic terminals are used as an axo-axonic marker. Catalog metadata lists bioRxiv; the PDF is the iScience article (29, 115624).

plain_language_summary: Some synapses land on the outgoing cable of a neuron rather than on its branches, and can strongly change whether a spike leaves the brain. Using the fly’s ventral-cord wiring map, this team finds those contacts on descending neurons and shows that a small set of ascending cells can make the giant escape neurons easier to fire.

ocar.opportunity: Memory engrams are thought to live in experience-dependent circuit plasticity, but the nanoscale synaptic architecture of an identified hippocampal ensemble has remained unresolved.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether neurons co-active during learning preferentially wire to one another, or whether other structural motifs store the trace.
ocar.action: Uytiepo, Zhu, Ellisman, Maximov and colleagues chemogenetically label ensembles recruited during associative learning and reconstruct the mouse hippocampal CA3–CA1 pathway with 3D electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: Neurons with a remote history of learning-related activity show no strong preference for wiring with each other; instead connectomes expand through multi-synaptic boutons independent of partner co-activation, with input-specific synapse upscaling and remodeling of mitochondria, smooth ER, and astrocyte interactions.
ocar.future_work: They note unknown temporal dynamics, possible early Hebbian phases seen with optical methods, Fos-threshold labeling bias, and the need to test other circuits and hippocampal axes.

summaries.beginner: A memory is supposed to live in a set of brain cells that fired together, but it was unclear how their connections actually change. In mouse hippocampus, this electron-microscope study finds that those cells do not mainly link to each other; they grow multi-contact boutons and enlarge selected synapses instead.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2025), Uytiepo and colleagues reconstruct the CA3–CA1 pathway after chemogenetic labeling of ensembles recruited during associative learning. Neurons whose activity history coincided with memory acquisition lacked a strong preference for wiring with one another. Rewiring proceeded through multi-synaptic boutons regardless of the co-activation state of postsynaptic partners, with spatially restricted, input-specific upscaling of individual synapses and organelle/astrocyte remodeling. The authors interpret these as physical hallmarks of long-term memory and a basis for flexible coding.
summaries.advanced: This is a nanoscale snapshot; temporal order is unresolved. Discrepancy with Fos-based trans-synaptic optical studies that reported early co-active CA3/CA1 preference is discussed as possibly a Hebbian then non-Hebbian sequence. “Activity” means above the Fos-induction threshold. Hallmarks were undetectable in pyramidal neurons activated by conditioned stimulus alone, which the authors use against a purely cell-type-intrinsic explanation. Generalization to other regions and to intelligence differences is speculative in the discussion.

plain_language_summary: A memory is supposed to live in a set of brain cells that fired together, but it was unclear how their connections actually change. In mouse hippocampus, this electron-microscope study finds that those cells do not mainly link to each other; they grow multi-contact boutons and enlarge selected synapses instead.

ocar.opportunity: Structural connectomes are increasingly complete, but a principled map from physical wiring to emergent function is still missing.
ocar.challenge: It remains unclear how to derive functional networks and neuron-level integrative roles from anatomical and extrasynaptic graphs without fitting a full biophysical simulator.
ocar.action: Moutuou and Benali introduce an algebraic quantum model: they treat the C. elegans anatomical and extrasynaptic connectomes as a directed multigraph, form its graph algebra, and identify functional networks with Kubo–Martin–Schwinger thermal equilibrium states.
ocar.resolution: Equilibrium states are used to define a functional connectome of topologically driven interactions and an Integration Capacity index that scores how neurons coordinate diverse information flows.
ocar.future_work: The framework is offered as a statistical, mechanistic account of information flow and as a way for connectome topology to predict cognition and complex behaviors.

summaries.beginner: We have a nearly complete wiring diagram of the worm, but not a simple rule that turns that diagram into functions such as sensing or crawling. This theory paper treats the wiring as a kind of quantum-inspired network and reads ‘functions’ off its equilibrium states.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 arXiv preprint (v3 dated 6 August 2025), Moutuou and Benali model C. elegans anatomical and extrasynaptic connectomes as a directed multigraph and derive an algebraic quantum system from the graph algebra. They identify functional networks with KMS thermal equilibrium states and introduce two outputs: a functional connectome of topology-driven interactions and an Integration Capacity (IC) index for each neuron’s coordination of information flow. They argue these features link network topology to cognition and behavior.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical/modeling paper; the selected extract does not report new physiology or a numerical prediction accuracy against calcium imaging. ‘Quantum’ here refers to algebraic/KMS formalism on a graph algebra, not to quantum biology of neurons. Catalog journal is blank; DOI 10.1103/jmqh-bqnc should be confirmed against a version of record. Claims that topology predicts complex behaviors should be read as a proposed account, not as a validated behavioral forecast in this extract.

plain_language_summary: We have a nearly complete wiring diagram of the worm, but not a simple rule that turns that diagram into functions such as sensing or crawling. This theory paper treats the wiring as a kind of quantum-inspired network and reads ‘functions’ off its equilibrium states.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can measure every synapse in a circuit, but not the dynamical parameters of every neuron and synapse, leaving open how much connectivity alone can explain computation.
ocar.challenge: Neither a wiring diagram nor a task specification uniquely determines mechanism, because different connectivities can implement the same computation and identical connectivity can function differently.
ocar.action: Lappalainen, Tschopp, Macke, Turaga and colleagues build a network with experimentally determined connectivity for 64 cell types in Drosophila optic-lobe motion pathways, leave single-neuron and synapse parameters free, and optimize those parameters with deep learning so the network detects visual motion.
ocar.resolution: The mechanistic model yields testable predictions for each neuron; predictions agreed with experimental measurements across 26 studies. They argue the strategy is more likely to succeed when neurons are sparsely connected, a widely observed biological feature.
ocar.future_work: They discuss adding sparse activity constraints, fitting to measured activity and behavior, and extending toward whole-animal models as optic-lobe and whole-fly connectomes proliferate.

summaries.beginner: We can now list every connection in a fly visual circuit, but we still do not know how strongly each cell responds or how fast each synapse is. This team freezes the real wiring, tunes the unknown knobs so the network detects motion, and finds that the predicted activity matches many published experiments.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Lappalainen and colleagues constrain a model to the measured connectivity of 64 cell types in fruit-fly optic-lobe motion pathways, then optimize unknown single-neuron and single-synapse parameters with deep learning so the network performs visual motion detection. Model predictions matched neural activity measurements reported across 26 studies. They present this as a strategy for generating detailed mechanistic hypotheses from connectivity plus a specified computation, especially in sparsely connected biological networks.
summaries.advanced: Agreement with 26 studies is a literature-comparison claim; the selected extract does not list which cell types failed. Parameters are optimized for a motion-detection task, not uniquely identified from data, so multiple parameter sets may remain (a point the introduction itself raises). Electrical synapses, neuromodulation, and glia are acknowledged as unmodeled. Success is argued to depend on sparse connectivity; dense circuits may remain degenerate. Nature volume/page in the extract: Vol. 634, 31 October 2024.

plain_language_summary: We can now list every connection in a fly visual circuit, but we still do not know how strongly each cell responds or how fast each synapse is. This team freezes the real wiring, tunes the unknown knobs so the network detects motion, and finds that the predicted activity matches many published experiments.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM yields connectomic ultrastructure but omits molecular labels needed to identify cell types, terminals, and channels in the same volume.
ocar.challenge: Conventional antibody CLEM needs detergents that wreck membranes for tracing, or post-embedding methods that are hard to multiplex in 3D.
ocar.action: Han, Lu, Trimmer, Lichtman and colleagues generate fluorescent single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) for detergent-free multiplex immunolabeling and volumetric CLEM, imaging six probes in female mouse cerebellum by spectral-unmixing confocal microscopy followed by vEM of the same sample.
ocar.resolution: They report excellent ultrastructure with multiple fluorescence channels, document a poorly described cell type, two mossy-fiber terminal types, and subcellular localization of one ion channel; eight scFv plasmids are deposited at Addgene.
ocar.future_work: Because scFvs can be derived from existing monoclonal antibodies (including NeuroMab collections), they argue hundreds of probes could support molecular overlays on connectomic volumes.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot show which molecular tags sit on which cells. This team makes small fluorescent antibody fragments that stain mouse cerebellum without punching holes in membranes, then takes both color pictures and an electron-microscope volume of the same piece of tissue.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Han and colleagues introduce multiplexed volumetric CLEM using fluorescent scFvs. They generated eight scFvs against brain markers and imaged six in a female mouse cerebellum with confocal spectral unmixing, then collected vEM on the same sample. The overlay yielded ultrastructure plus multiple molecular channels, revealing a poorly described cell type, two mossy-fiber terminal types, and the subcellular localization of one ion channel. Expression plasmids are in Addgene; probes carry a sortase tag for alternative labels.
summaries.advanced: The discussion refers to a volume labeled with five scFv probes in one place and six fluorescent probes in the abstract; check the figures for which channels were in the vCLEM volume. Biological identifications (cell type, terminal types, channel) are qualitative in the selected text, without counts. Multiplex power is illustrated with calbindin/parvalbumin logic for Purkinje versus molecular-layer interneurons. Expansion to ‘hundreds’ of probes is a prospect based on converting existing mAbs, not a library demonstrated here.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot show which molecular tags sit on which cells. This team makes small fluorescent antibody fragments that stain mouse cerebellum without punching holes in membranes, then takes both color pictures and an electron-microscope volume of the same piece of tissue.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-circuit connectomes invite ‘forward’ models that predict activity from wiring, but it is debated how strongly connectivity actually constrains dynamics.
ocar.challenge: Student–teacher networks that share a connectome can still differ in biophysical parameters, so a wiring diagram alone may leave recurrent dynamics degenerate.
ocar.action: Beiran and Litwin-Kumar develop a theory of connectome-constrained recurrent nets: a student with the same synaptic weights as a teacher but different unknown biophysical parameters is trained to match teacher activity.
ocar.resolution: A connectome often does not substantially constrain task-performing RNN dynamics; recordings from a small subset of neurons can remove that degeneracy. Solution spaces of constrained versus unconstrained models differ qualitatively, and the theory can prioritize which neurons to record.
ocar.future_work: They caution against over-interpreting underconstrained connectome models and note failure modes such as neuropeptides, gap junctions, synchrony codes, and unknown inputs.

summaries.beginner: Having a full wiring diagram does not automatically tell you how the network will fire, because each cell still has unknown speeds and strengths. This theory paper shows that a little bit of recorded activity from well-chosen cells can pin down the rest, while wiring alone often cannot.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2025), Beiran and Litwin-Kumar study student networks that inherit a teacher’s synaptic weights but not its biophysical parameters. Unlike unconstrained models, the unknown parameter count scales with neurons rather than synapses. They find that connectome constraints frequently leave dynamics underdetermined for a given task, yet sparse recordings can align student and teacher activity. The framework also ranks neurons by how much they would inform predictions. Analyses use synthetic networks and three empirical connectomes.
summaries.advanced: Catalog metadata lists a 2024 bioRxiv; the PDF is the 2025 Nature Neuroscience paper (28, 2561–2574). Robustness to model mismatch and synaptic-weight inaccuracy is claimed (Fig. 4 in the paper) but not numerically excerpted here. They assume known time-varying inputs and initial state; strongly input-driven activity with unknown inputs is not expected to be constrained. They did not apply the theory to C. elegans recordings, citing arguments that chemical synapses there may not predict functional interactions. Teacher activity on empirical connectomes used existing cell-type functional descriptions, not jointly aligned whole-brain recordings.

plain_language_summary: Having a full wiring diagram does not automatically tell you how the network will fire, because each cell still has unknown speeds and strengths. This theory paper shows that a little bit of recorded activity from well-chosen cells can pin down the rest, while wiring alone often cannot.

ocar.opportunity: A complete mouse-brain synaptic connectome would require uniform heavy-metal staining of a ~500 mm³ organ, far beyond established millimetre-scale protocols.
ocar.challenge: Whole-brain osmium staining faces slow infiltration, volume changes, cracks, and a tradeoff between ultrastructure and macroscopic integrity; methods that work on 1 mm³ punches or even >10 mm³ pieces do not automatically scale.
ocar.action: Lu, Wu, Schalek, Meirovitch, Berger, and Lichtman use time-lapse X-ray imaging and brain proxies to develop ODeCO, a 12-step osmium staining protocol, including pyrogallol conditioning with NaCl-matched osmolarity and a NaCl-based second osmication.
ocar.resolution: They report osmium infiltration throughout an entire mouse brain with preserved ultrastructure and without cracks or fragmentation, which they call a necessary prerequisite for a comprehensive mouse-brain connectome.
ocar.future_work: The preprint positions ODeCO as enabling later sectioning and EM of whole brains rather than delivering a reconstructed connectome.

summaries.beginner: To map every synapse in a mouse brain, the whole organ must be stained so membranes show up in the electron microscope—without splitting the tissue. This protocol uses X-ray movies of stain moving through the brain to time a twelve-step osmium recipe that the authors say soaks the entire brain without cracks.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint, Lu and colleagues introduce ODeCO, a 12-step staining strategy for whole-brain serial-section EM. They argue traditional osmium methods fail at mouse-brain scale (~500 mm³ versus prior ~1 mm³ Hua-style punches and recent >10 mm³ successes). Time-lapse X-ray and proxies guide reagent timing; pyrogallol replaces TCH for conditioning, with NaCl added to avoid a 17.8%±4.6% (n=3) volume expansion and cracking seen when switching into water. Sodium chloride rather than cacodylate shortens the second osmication from over 14 days to 6 days, while cacodylate is still recommended for the first osmication.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint, not a connectome. ‘Without any cracks or fragmentation’ is the authors’ claim for the protocol outcome; independent replication is not in the extract. The 17.8%±4.6% expansion is specifically for an unbuffered pyrogallol-in-water step, not for the final protocol. Second-osmication timing (14 versus 6 days) is for the buffer comparison they tested. Ultrastructural quality is asserted; the selected extract does not quote synapse-visibility metrics or a full-brain EM mosaic.

plain_language_summary: To map every synapse in a mouse brain, the whole organ must be stained so membranes show up in the electron microscope—without splitting the tissue. This protocol uses X-ray movies of stain moving through the brain to time a twelve-step osmium recipe that the authors say soaks the entire brain without cracks.

ocar.opportunity: Columnar visual systems are usually treated as mosaics of anatomically, genetically, and functionally uniform cell types, but some identified types violate functional uniformity.
ocar.challenge: Drosophila Tm9 is anatomically and genetically a single type yet has variable physiology; whether that variability comes from heterogeneous synaptic input was unknown.
ocar.action: Cornean, Molina-Obando, Silies and colleagues reconstruct presynaptic inputs of several hundred Tm9 cells across both optic lobes in FAFB/FlyWire, compare them with Tm1 and Tm2, and test wiring variability across animals with genetic synapse labeling and expansion microscopy.
ocar.resolution: Tm9 has three major plus many weak, sparsely distributed inputs, unlike Tm1/Tm2’s more stereotypic single major input; wide-field motifs are candidates for physiological diversity; heterogeneous wiring exists across individuals.
ocar.future_work: They argue visual systems may use distributed heterogeneous circuits for robust processing and that full visual connectomes can test how widespread such variability is.

summaries.beginner: The fly eye is usually described as 800 repeating columns with the same cell types doing the same jobs. One cell type, Tm9, breaks that rule: its wiring partners differ from column to column, which may explain why its electrical responses also vary.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Cornean and colleagues analyze Tm9 presynaptic connectivity in the FAFB volume using FlyWire, across both optic lobes. Tm9 has three major inputs and many weaker, sparsely distributed ones, whereas Tm1 and Tm2 have a single major, more stereotypic input. They identify motifs, including wide-field neurons, that could source Tm9’s variable physiology. Genetic synapse labeling with expansion microscopy indicates the heterogeneous wiring is not unique to one fly. They argue this distributed heterogeneity can support robust visual processing.
summaries.advanced: The abstract of the PDF does not repeat the expansion-microscopy clause that appears in the catalog abstract; both the FAFB analysis and across-individual labeling are in the paper. Spatial structure of variability is described as stochastic, without an apparent map. Cell-type status of Tm9 is defended on anatomy and genetics despite functional scatter; the authors warn that purely functional clustering might over-split types. Catalog metadata lists 2023 bioRxiv; the PDF is the 2024 Nature Communications article.

plain_language_summary: The fly eye is usually described as 800 repeating columns with the same cell types doing the same jobs. One cell type, Tm9, breaks that rule: its wiring partners differ from column to column, which may explain why its electrical responses also vary.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping proteins in the context of brain ultrastructure usually requires CLEM, which is slow and inaccessible compared with a confocal microscope.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy lacks ultrastructural context; EM lacks routine multiplex molecular labeling; super-resolution still does not paint dense neuropil the way membranes look in EM.
ocar.action: M’Saad, Bewersdorf, Kuan and colleagues introduce pan-ExM-t: about 16–24-fold linear expansion of tissue with fluorescent pan-stains of proteins and lipids plus immunolabeling of specific targets.
ocar.resolution: They image synaptic and cell-type antibodies in cultures and mouse brain sections in the context of pre- and postsynaptic densities, neuropil nanoarchitecture, and organelles, and they demonstrate tracing of neuronal circuitry from pan-ExM-t volumes.
ocar.future_work: They point to cryo-fixation, better lipid dyes, plasma-membrane stains for segmentation, in situ barcoding, and faster light-sheet microscopes as routes toward high-throughput optical connectomics.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes show the fine shape of brain tissue but not named proteins; ordinary microscopes show named proteins but not that fine shape. This method swells the tissue many times, stains all proteins and lipids so the scene looks EM-like, and still tags specific molecules—on a confocal microscope.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Biotechnology (2025; catalogued from a 2022 bioRxiv), M’Saad and colleagues present pan-expansion microscopy of tissue (pan-ExM-t). Linear expansion of ~16–24-fold is combined with fluorescent pan-staining (proteins and lipids) and immunolabeling. They demonstrate markers including Homer1, Bassoon, PSD-95, synaptophysin, GFAP, MBP, and GFP in dissociated neurons and mouse brain sections, revealing those labels beside synaptic densities and organelles. They also show circuit tracing from pan-ExM-t volumes and argue any lab with a confocal can adopt the method. Switching from beam-scanning to spinning-disk confocal yielded a ~12-fold imaging-speed gain in this study.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract quotes ~24-fold expansion and lists specific antibodies; the PDF abstract generalizes to ~16–24-fold and ‘synaptic and cell-specific antibodies.’ Tracing is demonstrated as a suggestion that optical connectomics is possible, not as a whole-circuit reconstruction. Pan-stain identity of every ultrastructural feature is still being characterized. Maleimide versus NHS ester pan-stains were not qualitatively different in tissue here. Author list on the PDF is expanded relative to the catalog row.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes show the fine shape of brain tissue but not named proteins; ordinary microscopes show named proteins but not that fine shape. This method swells the tissue many times, stains all proteins and lipids so the scene looks EM-like, and still tags specific molecules—on a confocal microscope.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM reconstructions are accelerating via automatic segmentation, but that accuracy often stalls on the preceding alignment of 2D sections into a 3D stack—especially at petascale.
ocar.challenge: Artifacts, missing sections, and the cost of global optimization make precise, robust alignment of whole brains or cubic millimetres difficult.
ocar.action: Popovych, Macrina, Seung and colleagues present a pipeline: self-supervised convolutional nets trained by metric learning to encode and align pairs, iterative fine-tuning, vector voting against artifacts, block-wise distributed alignment, and composing transformations with decay instead of a global solve.
ocar.resolution: Applied to a whole fly brain (FAFB), the pipeline improved accuracy relative to prior state of the art and scaled to a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex (MICrONS). Two open-source Python packages (including metroem and Corgie) are released.
ocar.future_work: The work is a production alignment system; several authors disclose financial interests in Zetta AI LLC.

summaries.beginner: Before computers can color neurons in a stack of electron-microscope slices, those slices must be lined up. This paper’s software learns to align neighboring pictures, votes to ignore damaged patches, and stitches blocks of a whole fly brain—and a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex—without a slow whole-volume optimization.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024; from a 2022 bioRxiv), Popovych and colleagues describe a petascale ssEM alignment pipeline. Self-supervised convnets initialize pairwise alignment; vector voting adds robustness to artifacts or missing data; the series is split into blocks for distributed workers; blocks are joined by composing transformations with decay. They report improved accuracy on FAFB relative to prior art and demonstrate scaling to MICrONS mouse visual cortex. Software is public (metroem, Corgie).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract does not quote a numeric alignment-error table versus named baselines. Author contributions assign FAFB coarse/fine alignment and mouse-cortex/MICrONS runs to specific coauthors. Competing interests: Seung, Kemnitz, Popovych, and Macrina disclose financial interests in Zetta AI LLC. Catalog metadata lists bioRxiv 2022; the PDF is the 2024 Nature Communications article (15:289).

plain_language_summary: Before computers can color neurons in a stack of electron-microscope slices, those slices must be lined up. This paper’s software learns to align neighboring pictures, votes to ignore damaged patches, and stitches blocks of a whole fly brain—and a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex—without a slow whole-volume optimization.

ocar.opportunity: Posterior parietal cortex shows choice-selective activity during decision-making, but how that selectivity is implemented in synaptic wiring was unknown.
ocar.challenge: Without jointly measured activity and synapse-resolution connectivity in the same neurons, models with selective versus non-selective inhibition could not be distinguished.
ocar.action: Kuan, Bondanelli, Harvey, Lee, Panzeri and colleagues combine virtual-reality behavior, two-photon calcium imaging, high-throughput serial TEM, and circuit modeling in mouse PPC.
ocar.resolution: Excitatory pyramids preferentially target inhibitory interneurons of the same selectivity; those interneurons preferentially target pyramids of opposite selectivity, forming an opponent-inhibition motif that models show amplifies selective inputs and improves trial-type encoding.
ocar.future_work: They note a modest sample of functionally characterized neurons, missing synapses outside the volume, and caution that synapse-size versus strength correlations are best established for E-to-E connections.

summaries.beginner: When a mouse chooses left or right, some parietal neurons fire for one choice. This study lines up those recordings with an electron-microscope wiring map and finds a push–pull motif: cells that like the same choice excite local inhibitors, which then suppress the opposite-choice cells.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Kuan and colleagues analyze mouse PPC during a virtual-reality decision task with two-photon imaging followed by large-volume serial TEM of the same tissue. Excitatory-to-inhibitory connections are more frequent and larger among co-selective pairs; inhibitory-to-excitatory connections are more frequent onto anti-selective pyramids. Circuit models indicate that this opponent-inhibition motif amplifies selective inputs, induces competition between opposite-selectivity populations, and improves encoding of trial type.
summaries.advanced: Sample size of functionally characterized neurons and within-volume synapses is described as modest; arbors and synapses outside the EM block are missing. No difference in I-to-E synapse size between co- and anti-selective pairs was detected. Synapse-size interpretation is caveated because size–strength correlation in cortex has been directly measured mainly for E-to-E synapses. The motif is contrasted with reports of non-selective E-to-I connectivity in mouse V1. Catalog metadata lists 2022 bioRxiv; the PDF is Nature 627, 367–373 (2024). A GridTape-related patent/licensing disclosure involves Lee, Hildebrand, and Graham.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks segment EM volumes well except where consecutive sections are missing, which splits neurons across the gap and creates a dedicated proofreading problem.
ocar.challenge: UNet data augmentation can hide a few lost slices, but large consecutive gaps leave fragment identity as a matching problem that voxel methods handle poorly and expensively.
ocar.action: Berman, Chklovskii, and Wu represent neuron fragments as point clouds and train CurveNet, a point-cloud classifier, to decide which fragments should be merged across the gap.
ocar.resolution: They report strong performance that scales to gaps larger than prior methods attempted, using far less data than voxel approaches would need, and they argue point clouds are a viable representation for other proofreading tasks.
ocar.future_work: They suggest extending the method to merged and split neurons throughout entire datasets.

summaries.beginner: When several electron-microscope slices in a row are unusable, automatic neuron coloring breaks into pieces above and below the hole. This paper turns those pieces into sparse 3D point clouds and trains a geometric network to guess which pieces belong to the same cell.
summaries.intermediate: In a MIDL 2022 submission (arXiv 2021), Berman, Chklovskii, and Wu treat gap-crossing fragment agglomeration as point-cloud classification with CurveNet. Consecutive missing sections are a common ssEM defect; they argue point-cloud representations remain accurate with an amount of data that would be unfeasible for competing methods and scale to larger gaps than prior work attempted. Keywords frame the task as neuron-fragment agglomeration and deep geometric learning.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract does not report accuracy percentages, gap thicknesses in sections, or named baseline scores. ‘Scales reasonably to gaps well beyond what other methods have attempted’ is the authors’ qualitative claim. The paper is a conference/arXiv methods piece, not a deployed whole-dataset proofreader. Catalog venue is the International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning; uuid in the catalog is the work_id because no DOI is stored.

ocar.opportunity: Animal tissues are networks of synaptic, chemical, and adhesive links; for muscles, desmosomes transmit force, but whole-body adhesive networks have not been mapped like neuronal connectomes.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown how hundreds of diverse muscles in an appendage-bearing larva attach to epithelia, glia, chaetae, and basal lamina, or how motoneuron synapses map onto that force network.
ocar.action: Jasek, Verasztó, Jékely and colleagues skeletonize 853 muscle cells and their desmosomal partners in a whole Platynereis larva volume-EM dataset and overlay motoneuron synapses.
ocar.resolution: They obtain a desmosomal connectome of over 2,000 cells; aciculae are highly connected hubs, matching their many degrees of freedom in video microscopy; motoneuron synapses let them infer tissue territories influenced by each motor class. The larva has 853 muscles of 53 types versus 95 similar body-wall muscles in C. elegans and 36 muscles of 10 types in Ciona tadpoles.
ocar.future_work: Together with the synaptic connectome from the same volume, they present the larva as a system for modeling crawling and parapodial motor control.

summaries.beginner: Muscles do not float; they glue to skin, bristles, and skeleton-like rods through tiny adhesive junctions. This team maps every such glue point in a whole marine-worm larva and shows that the internal bristle rods are the busiest attachment hubs, matching how freely those rods move on video.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint (October 2022 version), Jasek and colleagues reconstruct a whole-body desmosomal connectome in a Platynereis larva. Skeletonizing 853 muscle cells and partners yields a network of over 2,000 cells linking muscles to epithelial, glial, ciliated, and chaetal cells and basal lamina. Aciculae emerge as hubs, consistent with video-microscopy degrees of freedom. Mapping motoneuron synapses onto this adhesive graph infers the tissue domain each motoneuron can influence. Muscle diversity (53 types) is contrasted with C. elegans and Ciona.
summaries.advanced: ‘Connectome’ here means adhesive junctions, not chemical synapses, though motoneuron synapses are overlaid from the same volume (Verasztó et al. 2020). Stereotypy across segments is used to infer a specified connectivity code; that is an anatomical observation, not a developmental mechanism. Functional interpretations of attachments to ciliary cells are explicitly speculative. The selected extract does not quote synapse or desmosome counts beyond the cell totals (853 muscles; >2,000 cells; 53 types).
